title: New Partnership Launches First Collaborative Conservation Project
excerpt: Mahurangi West Pest is excited to announce the signing of a three-year Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the Auckland Council, formalising our partnership to restore and protect Mahurangi West and its Regional Parks.
html:
Mahurangi West Pest is excited to announce the signing of a three-year Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the Auckland Council, formalising our partnership to restore and protect Mahurangi West and its Regional Parks.

While Mahurangi West Pest has built a strong community-led pest control network across more than 3,500 hectares of private land, Auckland Council manages the neighbouring Regional Parks. This partnership recognises that effective conservation doesn’t stop at property boundaries. By working together across public and private land, we can create healthier habitats, strengthen native wildlife populations, and achieve even greater conservation outcomes for the Mahurangi West peninsula.

The first initiative under this new partnership is the Mahurangi West Coastal Wildlife Monitoring Project – Coast Guardians

Training by local Ranger Jared is on the 5th September at 9am, meet at top of Sullivans Bay.

This exciting community project will bring together volunteers to monitor sections of the Mahurangi West coastline throughout the breeding season. Participants will help record the presence and breeding activity of kororā (little blue penguins), nesting shorebirds and other coastal wildlife, while also noting threats such as predator activity and human disturbance.

The information collected will help build a valuable long-term picture of our local wildlife, allowing us to better understand the benefits of predator control and guide future conservation work.

In the coming weeks we’ll be inviting volunteers to attend a training session led by Auckland Council’s Community Ranger, Jared Anderson, before adopting a section of coastline to monitor throughout the season.

Whether you’re an experienced conservation volunteer or simply enjoy spending time exploring our beautiful coastline, we’d love to have you involved. To register your interest please email mahurangiwestpest@gmail.com

Why this matters

  • 🐧 Monitor & Record nesting sea and shorebirds
  • 🤝 Bring the community together
  • 🌿 Measure the long-term impact of predator control

title: Celebrating Our Trappers: Mahurangi West Pest Appreciation Event
excerpt: On Saturday 15 August, Mahurangi West Pest held our annual Trappers Appreciation Event, bringing together volunteers and supporters for an evening of celebration and thanks.
html:
On Saturday 15 August, Mahurangi West Pest held our annual Trappers Appreciation Event, bringing together volunteers and supporters for an evening of celebration and thanks.

Our trapping volunteers are a vital part of the conservation work happening across Mahurangi West. Week after week, they check traps, maintain equipment, respond to pest activity and help protect the native wildlife and habitats that make our area so special.

Over the past year, our community has achieved some fantastic results:

  • 3,791 pest animals removed – an average of 73 every week
  • 172 new pest-control tools added to our network
  • 3,500 hectares protected

These numbers represent an enormous amount of community effort, and the appreciation event was a chance to recognise the people behind those results.

Learning About Bird Flu

One of the highlights of the evening was a very informative presentation from Dr Jean Gulbransen, General Manager at Animates Vetcare, who spoke to us about Avian Influenza (H5N1), commonly known as bird flu.

Jean covered what bird flu is and where it came from, how it can spread and how it has reached New Zealand. She also explained why H5N1 is a significant concern, the signs and symptoms to be aware of, possible exposure and who may be at risk, as well as practical ways to help prevent exposure.

The presentation was particularly relevant for our volunteers, who regularly work outdoors and around wildlife. It provided a valuable opportunity to improve our understanding of H5N1 and the importance of good hygiene and biosecurity when working in the environment.

Conservation in Our Local Parks

We were also pleased to have Jared Anderson, our local park ranger, join us to provide an update on conservation work happening across Mahurangi West and Te Muri Regional Parks.

Jared shared some of the exciting restoration and pest-control work underway, including ongoing planting, stream restoration, weed control and the expansion of the pest-control network.

He also highlighted some of the special wildlife being seen across the parks, including Reef herons, Australasian bittern (matuku-hūrepo), Caspian terns and other threatened species.

It was great to hear about the progress being made in our local parks and the continued efforts to protect and restore these important areas.

Recognising Our Volunteers

A special part of the evening was recognising three volunteers who have made outstanding contributions to our trapping network.

🏆Volunteer Trapper of the Year – Mike Neil

Mike was recognised for his almost six years of dedication to Mahurangi West Pest. As a Hub Coordinator and a Lead Pest Controller, he has played an important role in supporting our trapping network and helping others develop their skills.

Mike brings enormous practical knowledge to the group and is always looking for ways to improve our trapping systems. His willingness to repair, modify and develop equipment, share his knowledge and find practical solutions has made a significant contribution to our predator-control programme.

Congratulations, Mike!

🏆 Rookie Trapper Award – Keegan Tinsel

Keegan received the Rookie Trapper Award in recognition of his enthusiasm, commitment and willingness to learn.

Since joining our trapping team, Keegan has quickly developed his skills and shown a genuine interest in understanding predator control. He has particularly embraced the technical side of trapping and has become a reliable and enthusiastic member of the team.

It’s fantastic to see new people developing their skills and becoming part of the next generation of conservation volunteers.

Congratulations, Keegan!

🏆 Volunteer Rookie of the Year – Suzie Baartz

Suzie was recognised for the enthusiasm, energy and commitment she brings to her trapping work at Waha Ridge.

She has quickly become an enthusiastic member of the trapping team, showing impressive attention to detail and determination when dealing with pest activity. Her commitment to learning, her willingness to get stuck in and her enthusiasm for seeing results have made her a fantastic addition to our volunteer network.

Congratulations, Suzie!

Thank You to Our Supporters

We are incredibly grateful to the local businesses who helped make the evening possible.

Pizza Hut Warkworth generously donated pizzas for our volunteers, providing a fantastic meal for everyone to enjoy.

Puhoi Valley generously donated cheese, which we used as part of the gift bundles presented to our award recipients, as well as putting some on the table for everyone to share and enjoy.

Bunnings Silverdale generously donated a $100 voucher, which helped us purchase important safety equipment for our volunteers.

New World Orewa also generously provided a $100 voucher, which helped us purchase food and drinks for the evening.

We are very grateful for the support of local businesses that help us look after the people who are working to protect our environment.

Thank You to Our Volunteers

Most importantly, thank you to every one of our volunteers.

Whether you are checking a trap every month, maintaining a trapline, helping at a planting day, controlling pest plants, monitoring wildlife or simply lending a hand when needed, your contribution matters.

Conservation is a team effort, and the results we are seeing across Mahurangi West are only possible because so many people are willing to give their time and energy.

We are incredibly proud of what our community has achieved together, and we look forward to another year of protecting, restoring and caring for Mahurangi West.

title: Auckland Council Renews Support for Community Coordinator Role
excerpt: Mahurangi West Pest is incredibly grateful to Auckland Council for its continued support through the Regional Environment and Natural Heritage (RENH) Grant Programme.
html:
Mahurangi West Pest is incredibly grateful to Auckland Council for its continued support through the Regional Environment and Natural Heritage (RENH) Grant Programme.

We are delighted to have secured $18,500 towards funding our Community Coordinator and Facilitator role for another year. As interest in community conservation continues to grow, having a dedicated coordinator ensures we can support more volunteers, respond to new opportunities, and build on the momentum that has already been created across Mahurangi West

The RENH Grant Programme received a high number of quality applications this year, making the funding round particularly competitive. We are therefore especially pleased that our project was recognised and supported, reflecting the strength of our community-led approach to conservation.

While Mahurangi West Pest is powered by volunteers, coordinating a growing community conservation programme requires dedicated planning, organisation, and communication. Funding for our Community Coordinator and Facilitator role provides the support needed to keep projects running smoothly, strengthen community participation, and ensure volunteers have the guidance and resources they need to make a lasting impact.

The role is responsible for coordinating volunteers, organising community events and restoration projects, supporting community-led initiatives, and fostering collaboration across the peninsula. It also focuses on securing additional funding, developing partnerships with organisations such as Auckland Council, The Forest Bridge Trust, Restore Rodney East, and Mahurangi Regional Park, and keeping our community informed through newsletters, annual reports, and our website.

Over the coming year, this funding will help us continue expanding our volunteer network, supporting landowners and community members, delivering restoration projects, strengthening partnerships, and securing additional funding to grow our work even further.

Auckland Council’s investment in community-led conservation extends far beyond financial support. Through ongoing advice, training opportunities, and collaboration, the Council continues to play an important role in helping groups like ours achieve lasting environmental outcomes.

We sincerely thank Auckland Council for its continued confidence in Mahurangi West Pest and the work of our dedicated volunteers. We’d also like to extend a special thank you to Rebecca Kemp for her ongoing support, guidance, and encouragement. Together, we’re making a real difference for nature and helping protect the biodiversity of Mahurangi West for future generations.

title: Thank you to Auckland Council
excerpt: A huge THANK YOU to Auckland Council for their generous support of invasive weed control in the buffer zone surrounding Mahurangi Regional Park. Their $10,000 grant to Mahurangi West Pest, awarded in January, has enabled us to carry out this important work.
html:
A huge THANK YOU to Auckland Council for their generous support of invasive weed control in the buffer zone surrounding Mahurangi Regional Park. Their $10,000 grant to Mahurangi West Pest, awarded in January, has enabled us to carry out this important work.

With this support, Mahurangi West Pest works alongside landowners and residents to control some of our most invasive pest plants, including wild ginger and asparagus fern, before they take over. This helps protect our native plants, supports the birds and wildlife that depend on them, and preserves the biodiversity that makes this area so special.

Every property involved helps protect Mahurangi Regional Park for future generations. Thank you to everyone who has participated so far 

If you live within the 500 m buffer zone around the regional park and would like to find out more or get involved, please email us at mahurangiwestpest@gmail.com.

title: Thank You, Huawai Bay Volunteers!
excerpt: A huge thank you to everyone who joined us at the Huawai Bay Restoration Project working bee. It was fantastic to see more than 60 members of our community and whānau come together to help restore this special area.
html:
A huge thank you to everyone who joined us at the Huawai Bay Restoration Project working bee. It was fantastic to see more than 60 members of our community and whānau come together to help restore this special area.

Together, volunteers achieved an incredible amount in just one day. A large volume of invasive vegetation was cleared, chipped, and mulched, and approximately 1,300 native plants were planted across the site.

This working bee was an important milestone in the wider Huawai Bay / 35 Jamieson Road reforestation project. Thanks to the combined efforts of contractors, volunteers, community members, and whānau, around 90% of the invasive weed and unwanted tree removal has now been completed. More than three tonnes of ginger bulbs and almost four tonnes of other invasive weeds have been removed, helping to create the space needed for native plants to thrive.

A special thank you goes to our project leaders, Hugh and Pete, whose planning, coordination, and hard work has made this project such a success. Their dedication, along with the enthusiasm of everyone involved, has been instrumental in driving this project forward.

Since this planting day, the project has reached another exciting milestone. From mid-July all 5,155 native plants will be planted—a fantastic achievement made possible by the collective efforts of everyone involved.

There is still more work to do, with a weeding and firewood/pine cone clean up community working bee planned once the logging has been completed. We look forward to seeing another great turnout as we continue restoring Huawai Bay together.

Ngā mihi nui to everyone who has contributed their time, energy, and support. Your efforts are making a lasting difference for our local environment and future generations.

title: Kākā Making a Comeback in Mahurangi West
excerpt: Our June quarterly bird count is now underway. These surveys help us track changes in bird populations across Mahurangi West. Photograph from Department of Conservation website
html:
Our June quarterly bird count is now underway. These surveys help us track changes in bird populations across Mahurangi West.

Photograph from Department of Conservation website

One encouraging story to emerge from the bird counts has been the return of the Kākā. During the first two years of surveys, there were no reports of Kākā in the area. They then began appearing occasionally, and now feature in virtually every quarterly report. Many of you may have seen or heard these distinctive native parrots. Even more exciting, kākā successfully raised chicks in the Bullock Track area last summer.

Kākā are particularly vulnerable to predators such as rats, stoats and possums, especially when nesting. Possums also eat the same kind of food as Kākā, most significantly, high energy food types such as endemic mistletoe and Rātā. The growing presence of Kākā in Mahurangi West is a strong sign that sustained pest control is helping create a safer environment for native wildlife. It is a wonderful reminder that our collective efforts are making a real difference.

To read more on the Kākā visit https://www.doc.govt.nz/nature/native-animals/birds/birds-a-z/kaka/

title: Titī – Cook’s Petrel Research
excerpt: The Seabird Trust is collecting reports of Cook’s Petrel (tītī) calls, heard as they fly across the Auckland Isthmus / North Auckland Isthmus. Because of their kek-kek-kek calls, these birds have been dubbed ‘flying goats’. You can help the tītī (and NZ fairy tern) on their mainland flyway by tracking them across Auckland as they fly between…
html:
The Seabird Trust is collecting reports of Cook’s Petrel (tītī) calls, heard as they fly across the Auckland Isthmus / North Auckland Isthmus. Because of their kek-kek-kek calls, these birds have been dubbed ‘flying goats’. You can help the tītī (and NZ fairy tern) on their mainland flyway by tracking them across Auckland as they fly between the Tasman Sea and Hauraki Gulf.

There are several aims: to better understand these seabirds, raise public awareness, highlight seasonality and the risk to fledglings departing colonies, and to promote the

reduction of artificial light at night to mitigate threats to them and other species.

You can add your own ‘research’ using the programme’s online form: such as the number of ‘Times when you heard a petrel or petrels on one night’.

Jared Anderson, park ranger at Mahurangi Regional Park, says that he often hears the calls of the tītī over Sullivan’s Bay. The tītī breed from October to April, with the peak of calling by birds flying overland occurring from October to January each year.

For more information on how to join the programme go to:

https://www.nzseabirdtrust.com/our-species-projects

title: Feral Cats Added To 2050 Hitlist
html:
BREAKING NEWS …

On 20 November, Conservation Minister Tama Potaka announced that feral cats would be added to the Predator Free 2050 hitlist. Describing feral cats as “stone cold killers”, Potaka said that they would “join their buddies, stoats, ferrets, weasels – mustelids, rats and possums” on the official list for eradication. It marks the first change to the list of pest species since the target’s inception in 2016.

title: Hub Coordinator Roles
excerpt: What does a month in the life of a hub coordinator look like? Have you got what it takes to be a part-time volunteer hub coordinator? We have 9 hubs, each with a coordinator who looks after the needs of trappers in his or her area.
html:
What does a month in the life of a hub coordinator look like? Have you got what it takes to be a part-time volunteer hub coordinator? We have 9 hubs, each with a coordinator who looks after the needs of trappers in his or her area.

As a coordinator you will receive goodies – lures, bait, etc – from our lead coordinators, to distribute to volunteer trappers in your hub, when they need restocking. Once a month you’ll ask your trappers how their supplies are, and for any general trapping issues. And you’ll keep your ear to ground in case someone new in the area wants to trap.

You will help lay and set up new traplines or add or replace traps, and of course once you’re up to speed, give training and support to others, such as how to lay a flour blaze to attract possums. Or the importance of trap hygiene and maintenance.

Wanted: A Volunteer Coordinator for Hub 5 (South Mahurangi West)

Contact our lead coordinator Jeff [mob. 027 590 9245] if you’d like to discuss becoming a pest control hub coordinator for either Hub 5 or Hub 8 (see maps below).

title: A Month of Weed Cafes
excerpt: Despite the hot, dry conditions throughout May 2025, our volunteers rolled up their sleeves over four consecutive Sundays. Our 1-HR Weed Cafés saw community members weeding, mulching and watering native plants at Jamieson Bay and the top of Ōpahi Bay Road, giving them the best chance of surviving the dry spell.
html:
Despite the hot, dry conditions throughout May 2025, our volunteers rolled up their sleeves over four consecutive Sundays. Our 1-HR Weed Cafés saw community members weeding, mulching and watering native plants at Jamieson Bay and the top of Ōpahi Bay Road, giving them the best chance of surviving the dry spell.

The prolonged lack of rain meant our young native plantings needed extra care. Weeds compete with young plants for limited water and nutrients, making regular maintenance especially important during dry weather. By removing competing weeds, applying a generous layer of mulch to retain soil moisture, and watering with added nutrients, volunteers helped reduce stress on the plants and improve their chances of establishing strong root systems.

Our 1-HR Weed Cafés continue to be a fantastic way for people to contribute, whether they’re regular volunteers or joining us for the first time. Spending just an hour outdoors not only makes a real difference to our restoration sites but is also a great opportunity to meet others in the community who share a passion for protecting our local environment.

A huge thank you to everyone who joined us throughout the month. Every hour volunteered helps build healthier native forests that will provide habitat for birds, insects and other wildlife for generations to come.

Photograph below: MWP volunteers cleared the corner site of rubbish, kikuya and brush wood, back in October 2022.

title: Possum Traps from Predator Free NZ
excerpt: Jeff Marsh, Pest Control Manager for Mahurangi West Pestwith a new delivery of Predator Free NZ pest control tools
html:
Jeff Marsh, Pest Control Manager for Mahurangi West Pest
with a new delivery of Predator Free NZ pest control tools

Our Pest Control Manager, Jeff Marsh, takes charge of a new delivery of 34 Flipping Timmy possum traps and 3 Trapinators (another type of possum trap), purchased with a generous grant from Predator Free NZ, as part of its Backyard Communities programme. These humane traps will be used in our coastal communities to reduce the numbers of possums devastating the eggs and chicks of native birds in particular, but also a wide range of plants, from fruit trees, to flowering natives. Possums eat up to 3 kilograms each, per night, of leaves, shoots and fruit.

title: A Myna Discussion
excerpt: Recognised for its detrimental impact on biodiversity, the Myna bird is listed by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) as one of the world’s most aggressively invasive avian species.
html:
Recognised for its detrimental impact on biodiversity, the Myna bird is listed by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) as one of the world’s most aggressively invasive avian species.

Why Mynas are a problem

Mynas are territorial and aggressive toward other birds and have been known to remove native species from their nests for their own use. Where mynas gather in large numbers to feed on stock food, crops or fruit, they cause considerable economic loss.

< Photo Credit: Ormon Torr

The myna also poses risks to agricultural crops and carries diseases such as avian influenza and malaria, which could potentially lead to the extinction of some local bird species, according to a 2009 study.

On Sunday, twelve community volunteers braved the weather to dig in 144 native ground cover plants on the near vertical site on the edge of the Jamieson Bay Esplanade Reserve. Plants included native flax, astelia, Hebe, Daphne and iris.

Above: Dan Marrow, a park ranger with the Rodney Local Board, unloads trays of healthy native plants which his organisation donated for our coastal rehabilitation project.

Above: Our team of volunteers made short work of the weeds and rubbish like the faded old cone pictured. Once the plants were in the ground, there was just time for a BBQ, also delivered along with the plants by Dan Marrow (Rodney Local Board), before the rain set in.

Above: The flyer for this event was designed by volunteer Michelle Spooner.

Stoats and other mustelids will eat native and endemic birds, their chicks and eggs,
invertebrates, rodents, lizards, hedgehogs and fish. They are carnivores and only eat other animals. Stoats can climb trees and swim a few kilometres, and they hunt day and night.

In celebration of the first ever national public holiday for Matariki on June 24, an invited contingent boarded boats at Sandspit for the short trip out to Motu Reka Reka and Motu Kete Kete. These islands lie off Martins Bay, just north of the mouth of the Mahurangi Harbour.

Ngāti Manuhiri Settlement Trust, working in collaboration with Revive Our Gulf as kaitiaki and tiaki, has a mission to restore te moana with a focus on their rohe or tribal areas. Ngāti Manuhiri is dedicated to deploying 150 tonnes of kūtai (mussel spat) sustainably and effectively into te moana in order to regenerate mussel beds.

Representatives from many of the organisations contributing to and supporting the program took part in the ceremonial deployment of mussels on the day.

html:
Myna Control

In New Zealand alphachloralose is commonly used for the control of sparrows, pigeons, blackbirds, mynas and magpies. Alphachloralose is a narcotic and when used in concentrations of less than 2.5% it anaesthetises birds rather than kills them. Comatose birds are then collected and the pest species humanely killed. Non-target species can be revived by placing them in a warm dark place. Bait is available as treated wheat, barley and peas and as a paste. From Sustainable Options, Pest Animal Control 15, Bay of Plenty Regional Council

If you’d rather trap mynas, the Canberra Indian Myna Action Group designed the Pee Gee’s Myna trap specifically for Indian or common mynas and starlings. Clarence Valley Conservation in Action (CVCIA) in Australia made some modifications mainly for humane reasons, and use and recommend this trap design. Traps must be used in accordance with your local Animal Welfare Act and users must commit to the humane treatment and euthanasia of captured birds. It is extremely important that correct advice and procedures for trapping be sought and followed as incorrect technique can lead to trap shyness of birds and may compromise the trapping program for all. More information about trapping and the euthanasia of mynas is available at: www.indianmynaaction.org.au

title: Trapping data and collaboration
excerpt: Traps, bait and volunteers are all key in the effort to create a pest free peninsular, but one other very important aspect is ‘data’. Hear about how Trap.nz is supporting Mahu West Pest.
html:
words by Michelle Spooner

Traps, bait and volunteers are all key in the effort to create a pest free peninsular, but one other very important aspect is ‘data’.

Mahurangi West Pest began over three years ago, when Project Lead Brian Bramell decided to expand beyond his own back-yard trapping, creating a network of people in the community who wanted to see native birds thrive.

Bringing data into the project

In approaching Auckland Council to access traps for the project, Brian says they were able to make the commitment to provide some traps and tools on the condition that as a work group, Mahurangi West Pest would sign up to the Trap.nz mobile app for data collection.

The app not only allows pest control groups to plot traps, trap-lines and bait stations; it also records trapping data for monitoring and evaluation within projects.

Plotting and maintaining traps

Mahurangi West Pest Coordinator, Mike Neil says he and another coordinator, Jeff Marsh, have been using Trap.nz when they’ve been establishing new trap-lines.

Trap.nz has been a great way to plot the lines and ensure important parts of the landscape are not being missed, he says.

“For some of the trap-lines, we’re walking through really dense bush, but when we position each trap and log it with Trap.nz, the GPS gives us the exact location.”

Using Trap.nz also means the trap-line volunteers are able to locate the traps and ensure each are being checked regularly.

“Once in action, they can then record the number of kills, which pest is caught, what bait is working and how often the traps are being rebaited,” says Mike.

Part of a team

Mahurangi West Pest relies on each of its volunteers maintaining their traps on a regular basis.

In being a part of Trap.nz, and seeing the data it produces, says Mike, also helps to feel like you’re a part of team.

“We’re all trying to get these pests and we’re often working alone – but when you see the number of kills in the area and know that you’ve contributed to it, there’s a feel-good factor; that it can be achieved together,” he says.  

Beneficial for all parties

Recording the data, Brian says, has been mutually beneficial for both Mahu West Pest and Auckland Council.  

“We’ve been able to track and understand our work – and from a Council point, they can see the assets they’ve put into our project, and that they’re being used efficiently.

“They can see that we’re trapping and maintaining the traps effectively; which as a result, makes it easier for applying and approving funding to expand.”

Being part of the bigger picture

Developed by a New Zealand company, Trap.nz is being used by regional councils and community restoration projects to contribute towards the goal of Pest Fee Aotearoa 2050. By using Trap.nz, Mahurangi West Pest’s data is automatically combined with others across the country.   

Brian says he’s currently also networking with other local pest groups and is part of the wider support network, Restore Rodney East.

“Trap.nz allows these projects to share data and also make gap analysis to identify areas of land that are being missed,” says Brian.

“Ultimately pulling together as a team and having a coordinated effort is essential to make a difference,” he says.

Interested in joining Trap.nz? If you currently have traps and would like to join the Mahurangi West Pest project on Trap.nz to add your progress, we’d love to hear from you. Once joined, we can provide support with the best ways to set your traps, and in some cases, we can provide you with bait. For more information – check out our website Traps and target areas – mahurangiwestpest.wordpress.com

title: Find, research and protect native bat
excerpt: Mahu West Pest was recently successful in obtaining a $5,000 grant from Auckland Council Environmental Services for research into the long-tailed bat or pekapeka-tou-roa.
html:
published 9 February 2022

Mahu West Pest was recently successful in obtaining a $5,000 grant from Auckland Council Environmental Services for research into the long-tailed bat or pekapeka-tou-roa.

Bird of the Year

A few feathers were ruffled last year when the pekapeka-tou-roa was voted New Zealand’s Bird of the Year!  Peter Wills, Campaign Manager for the bat entry, says it was a matter of supporting the ‘underbird’, which has a status of ‘nationally threatened’ in conservation and received a bad rap from the Covid-19 pandemic.

Nationally, the awareness of the bats had been lifted, and Mahu West Pest saw an opportunity for bats which may call our community ‘home’.

Funding to help our local efforts  

Nada Cottrell, Mahu West Pest Funding Coordinator, says the team decided to apply for the funding grant and was successful in receiving $5,000 towards work to find and protect bats on the Mahurangi West peninsula.

She says their first objective, with the support of volunteers and the use of acoustic listening devices, is to be able to identify any bats that might be in the area.

“If found, we’ll then work to provide awareness for the community and training for volunteers in best practice to support our local bats.”

Long-term, Nada says, Mahu West Pest would like to help establish and maintain a viable long-tailed bat population on the peninsula.

Local volunteers and landowners

Mahu West Pest are now looking for local volunteers who would like to learn more about assisting with bat research in Mahurangi West, such as learning about acoustic listening devices for bats, and/or supporting bat habitats.

We also would like to hear from land-owners who are willing for on-the-ground research to take place on their land.

If you are interested, please contact: nada.mahuwestpest@gmail.com

How to help the bat

Information from Auckland Environmental Services suggest land owners can do the following to support our native bats:

  • Retain standing dead trees and old-age trees with cavities. Bats breed in cavities in old-aged trees, moving to a new roost tree regularly, returning later to reuse it. Social groups may use over 100 different roosting trees. If felling a woodlot, check trees for cavities first. 
  • Protect cabbage trees and other lone native trees on farmland as important roosts. Replant natives to shelter and ensure their long term survival.  
  • Protect old-age willow and mature natives around ponds where bats feed, e.g. aquatic insects over water. Overhanging trees around ponds help bats feed in poor weather.
  • Reduce the use of pesticides negatively impacting bats.

Bat Fact

A Long-tailed Bat (pekapeka-tou-roa) weighs about the same as New Zealand’s $2 coin.

title: A Year in Bird Counting
excerpt: As the last of the qarterly bird counts are completed for 2021, Fran Ashton, Mahu West Pest’s Lead Bird Counter provides us with an update
html:
Published December 2021

Words by Michelle Spooner

As the last of the quarterly bird counts are completed for 2021, Fran Ashton, Mahurangi West Pest’s Lead Bird Counter says it’s been great fun.

Fran has been a part of Mahurangi West Pest for the past two years and says her interest within the group has been around the bird life. 

“The monitoring of birds is one way for us to know how effectively trapping is working in the area,” says Fran.

“It’s a long-term investment – but it shows us which birds are benefiting [from the pest control] the most and which we need to put more focus into.”

Fran Ashton (above left) and bird watching at Takatu with fellow volunteers.

The counting

Fran says it will be 3-4 years from now before they will start to have enough counting data to really understand the impact of trapping on birdlife in Mahurangi West – and hopefully see a lot more native birds.

The counting so far has been based in Jamieson and Opahi Bays and the Bullock track – where four times a year they get out and count what they see and hear, for what takes about 15-20 minutes all up.

“Our monitoring is based on the DOC five-minute bird count form which is a recognised standard for bird monitoring where pest control is taking place in the same area,” says Fran. 

Once completed, Fran compiles the forms and enters the information onto the e-Birds website where the information is shared both in New Zealand and internationally.

This year’s learning

This first year has been a good learning curve with the support of Jared Anderson, local park ranger, as well as others says Fran.

“Sometimes you hear four different birds and distinguishing which is which has become a little easier each quarter,” she says.   

More and more locals are becoming interested which is good to see. Some of the exciting discoveries this year have been kākā, shining cuckoo, and a juvenile starling (identified with the support of Auckland Council’s Senior Ornithologist).

If you’re interested in becoming a bird counter with Mahurangi West Pest, get in touch with Fran at: ashton.sager@gmail.com

excerpt: You want to get involved and give back to the community, but can’t fit another big commitment into your busy schedule? Then microvolunteering might just be the thing. html:
You want to get involved and give back to the community, but can’t fit another big commitment into your busy schedule? Then microvolunteering might just be the thing.

Microvolunteering is a small, bite-sized task or project, that is quick and easy to perform. For example, it only takes 30 minutes to do a bird count, and just four times a year (to cover the four seasons). You could check a trap line (including resetting and baiting) in about half an hour. Checking community traps (where there are generally just 3-5) can be done in 15-20 minutes.
